Norfolk Coast: Where the Sky Is the Star

The Norfolk coast is unlike anywhere else in England. There are no dramatic cliffs, no towering headlands, no crashing Atlantic surf. Instead, there are vast salt marshes, endless beaches, enormous skies, and a quality of light that has drawn artists for centuries. For motorcyclists, Norfolk offers something rare — genuinely quiet roads through beautiful countryside, charming market towns, outstanding seafood, and a pace of life that makes you wonder why you ever rode anywhere else.

The Coast Road

The A149 from King's Lynn to Cromer is Norfolk's signature ride. Officially designated as part of the Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, this road threads through a succession of charming villages — Burnham Market, Wells-next-the-Sea, Blakeney, Cley-next-the-Sea, and Sheringham. The road is well-surfaced and gently flowing, with the marsh landscape opening out to the sea on your left. Take your time — this is not a road to rush.

Key Coastal Destinations

  • Wells-next-the-Sea — A picture-perfect harbour town with colourful beach huts, a narrow-gauge railway to the beach, and excellent crab sandwiches
  • Blakeney — Historic fishing village, famous for seal-watching boat trips to Blakeney Point, home to England's largest grey seal colony
  • Burnham Market — Known as "Chelsea-on-Sea" for its upmarket shops and galleries, but genuinely beautiful with its wide Georgian green
  • Cley-next-the-Sea — A birdwatcher's paradise with the Norfolk Wildlife Trust reserve, plus an excellent smokehouse selling local kippers
  • Cromer — A traditional seaside town famous for its pier and Cromer crab, considered the finest crab in England
  • Holkham — Vast beach backed by pine woods, and Holkham Hall, one of England's grandest Palladian mansions

The Broads

Inland from the coast, the Norfolk Broads offer a completely different landscape — a network of rivers, lakes, and marshes that forms Britain's largest protected wetland. The riding through the Broads is gentle and flat, through villages with round-towered churches and riverside pubs. Ranworth Broad has a floating wildlife centre. Hickling Broad is one of the best places in Britain to see marsh harriers and bitterns.

Norfolk doesn't shout. It whispers. And if you slow down enough to listen, you'll hear why painters, poets, and now motorcyclists keep coming back. The light here is different, the skies are bigger, and the seafood is remarkable.

Food and Drink

Norfolk's food scene is outstanding. Cromer crab is legendary — sweet, delicate, and best eaten as a simple dressed crab with brown bread. Brancaster mussels and Stiffkey cockles (known locally as "Stewkey Blues") are local specialities. The White Horse at Brancaster Staithe has a terrace overlooking the marshes — one of England's finest pub views. Morston Hall holds a Michelin star. Wells has several excellent fish-and-chip shops.

Beyond the Coast

Explore inland to find quiet lanes through rolling farmland dotted with magnificent medieval churches — Norfolk has more medieval churches than any other county in England. Castle Acre has a ruined Cluniac priory and Norman castle. Houghton Hall, Sir Robert Walpole's Palladian mansion, hosts world-class contemporary art exhibitions. The market town of Fakenham has a weekly Thursday market and a racecourse.

Practical Information

Norfolk is accessed via the A11 and A47 from the Midlands, or the A10/M11 from London — allow 3 hours from central London, 2.5 from Birmingham. King's Lynn makes a good western gateway, Cromer or Sheringham for the east. Fuel is available in all the main towns. Accommodation ranges from luxury boutique hotels in Burnham Market to campsites and B&Bs. Norfolk roads are generally flat and well-surfaced but can be narrow with high hedges — watch for agricultural vehicles. Best months: April to October, with May and September being ideal for lighter crowds and good weather. The seal pupping season at Blakeney Point peaks in November-January, which is a spectacular sight if you're willing to wrap up warm. faq.q: What is the best road on the Norfolk coast?
faq.a: The A149 from King's Lynn to Cromer is Norfolk's signature ride, part of the Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. It threads through a succession of charming villages including Burnham Market, Wells-next-the-Sea, Blakeney, Cley-next-the-Sea and Sheringham. The road is well-surfaced and gently flowing, with the marsh landscape opening to the sea. Take your time.

faq.q: Where can I see seals on the Norfolk coast?
faq.a: Blakeney is famous for seal-watching boat trips to Blakeney Point, home to England's largest grey seal colony. The seal pupping season peaks in November to January, which is a spectacular sight if you are willing to wrap up warm. Boat trips run year-round from Blakeney and Morston quays.

faq.a: Norfolk's food scene is outstanding. Cromer crab is legendary, sweet and delicate, best eaten simply dressed with brown bread. Brancaster mussels and Stiffkey cockles, known locally as Stewkey Blues, are local specialities. The White Horse at Brancaster Staithe has a terrace overlooking the marshes, and Morston Hall holds a Michelin star.

faq.a: Norfolk is accessed via the A11 and A47 from the Midlands, or the A10 and M11 from London, allowing three hours from central London and 2.5 from Birmingham. King's Lynn makes a good western gateway and Cromer or Sheringham the east. Fuel is available in all the main towns.

faq.q: When is the best time to ride the Norfolk coast?
faq.a: The best months are April to October, with May and September ideal for lighter crowds and good weather. If you want the seal pupping spectacle at Blakeney Point, visit in the November to January window instead.
